hypotheses.title: rebalanceSwap lets anyone drain userToken reserves to arbitrary recipient
hypotheses.description: rebalanceSwap() has no access control and no caller restriction, yet it moves userToken reserves out of the pool to an arbitrary `to` address chosen by the caller. Any external actor can call it, pay a small amount of validatorToken (amountIn = amountOut*N/SCALE + 1), and direct the userToken output to themselves. The function is intended for privileged rebalancing but is fully public.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker identifies a pool with userToken reserves. 2) Calls rebalanceSwap(userToken, validatorToken, amountOut = reserveUserToken, to = attacker). 3) Pays amountIn of validatorToken via transferFrom. 4) Receives the entire userToken reserve at `to`. 5) Repeats across pools.
hypotheses.impact: Complete drainage of userToken reserves from every pool; LPs lose their deposited userToken; pool becomes insolvent.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict rebalanceSwap to a trusted role (e.g., onlyValidator/onlyOwner) or require the caller to be an authorized rebalancer.

hypotheses.title: burn() transfers tokens before updating reserves and balances
hypotheses.description: In `burn()`, the contract performs `IERC20(userToken).transfer(to, amountUserToken)` and `IERC20(validatorToken).transfer(to, amountValidatorToken)` BEFORE decrementing `liquidityBalances[poolId][msg.sender]`, `totalSupply[poolId]`, and the pool reserves. If either token has a transfer hook (ERC-777, ERC-1155-like, or a malicious/upgradeable token), the recipient `to` can reenter `burn()` while its liquidity balance and the pool reserves are still unchanged, allowing the same liquidity to be redeemed repeatedly.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker mints liquidity in a pool whose userToken or validatorToken has a transfer callback (or deploys such a token as one side of a new pool). 2) Attacker calls `burn()` with `to` = attacker contract. 3) During `IERC20(userToken).transfer(to, ...)` (or validatorToken transfer), the token invokes the attacker's hook. 4) Hook reenters `burn()` with the same `liquidity`; the check `liquidityBalances[poolId][msg.sender] < liquidity` still passes because the decrement has not happened yet. 5) Repeat until pool reserves are drained.
hypotheses.impact: Complete drainage of pool reserves; other LPs lose funds; totalSupply and reserve accounting become inconsistent/insolvent.
hypotheses.recommendation: Apply checks-effects-interactions: decrement `liquidityBalances`, `totalSupply`, and pool reserves before performing the token transfers (or add a reentrancy guard).

hypotheses.title: FeeAMM executeFeeSwap uses unchecked ERC20 transfer return values
hypotheses.description: `IERC20(userToken).transferFrom(...)` and `IERC20(validatorToken).transfer(...)` return booleans that are ignored. If either token is a non-reverting ERC20 that returns false (e.g., some stablecoins or proxy tokens), the swap state updates (reserve changes) still occur even though no tokens moved. This desynchronizes pool reserves from actual balances.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker uses a userToken that returns false on transferFrom without reverting. 2) Attacker calls executeFeeSwap(); reserveUserToken is incremented and reserveValidatorToken decremented, and validatorToken is transferred out to attacker. 3) Attacker never actually paid userToken. 4) Attacker repeats to drain validatorToken reserves.
hypotheses.impact: Complete drain of validatorToken reserves; pool accounting corrupted.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use SafeERC20 or require the boolean return value of transfer/transferFrom.

hypotheses.title: Fee swap uses fixed rate ignoring pool reserves, enabling value extraction
hypotheses.description: executeFeeSwap computes amountOut = amountIn * M / SCALE (a fixed 99.7% rate) regardless of the pool's actual reserve ratio. The pool reserves are only used as a liquidity check, not to derive the exchange rate. This means the swap price is completely decoupled from the pool state, so any user can drain the validatorToken reserve at a favorable fixed rate whenever the true pool ratio deviates from M/SCALE.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a pool where reserveValidatorToken/reserveUserToken is much higher than M/SCALE (e.g., after a large rebalanceSwap or burn skewed the pool). 2) Attacker calls executeFeeSwap with a large amountIn. 3) Contract pays out amountIn*M/SCALE of validatorToken at the fixed rate, ignoring the actual pool ratio. 4) Attacker repeats until reserveValidatorToken is depleted or the ratio normalizes, extracting value from LPs.
hypotheses.impact: LPs lose funds as the pool is drained at a mispriced rate; pool can become insolvent or heavily imbalanced.
hypotheses.recommendation: Derive amountOut from the constant-product invariant using current reserves (e.g., amountOut = reserveValidatorToken * amountIn * M / (reserveUserToken * SCALE + amountIn * M)), not a fixed constant.

hypotheses.title: rebalanceSwap uses fixed rate ignoring reserves, enabling arbitrage drain
hypotheses.description: rebalanceSwap computes amountIn = amountOut * N / SCALE + 1, a fixed 99.85% rate, independent of the pool's reserve ratio. The only reserve check is pool.reserveUserToken >= amountOut. An attacker can repeatedly extract userToken at a fixed price whenever the pool's true ratio differs from N/SCALE, draining the userToken reserve.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker finds a pool where reserveUserToken/reserveValidatorToken is much higher than SCALE/N (i.e., userToken is cheap relative to the fixed rate). 2) Attacker calls rebalanceSwap with amountOut set to a large value. 3) Contract charges only amountOut*N/SCALE+1 of validatorToken and pays out amountOut of userToken at the fixed rate. 4) Repeat until reserveUserToken is drained.
hypotheses.impact: userToken reserve drained at mispriced rate; LPs suffer loss of funds and pool becomes imbalanced/insolvent.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute amountIn from the constant-product invariant using current reserves rather than a fixed constant.

hypotheses.title: rebalanceSwap() updates reserves before pulling validatorToken, enabling reentrancy
hypotheses.description: `rebalanceSwap()` increments `pool.reserveValidatorToken` and decrements `pool.reserveUserToken` BEFORE calling `IERC20(validatorToken).transferFrom(...)` and `IERC20(userToken).transfer(to, amountOut)`. A malicious `validatorToken` (or one with hooks) can reenter during `transferFrom`, and a malicious `userToken` can reenter during `transfer(to, ...)`. Because reserves are already mutated but the incoming `amountIn` has not actually been received, the pool's accounting is temporarily inconsistent and reentrant calls (e.g., `executeFeeSwap`, `burn`, or another `rebalanceSwap`) can exploit the skewed reserves.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates/uses a pool where `validatorToken` is a token they control with a `transferFrom` hook. 2) Attacker calls `rebalanceSwap(userToken, validatorToken, amountOut, to)`. 3) Reserves are updated (validator reserve up, user reserve down) before the token pull. 4) During `transferFrom`, the hook reenters `executeFeeSwap` or `burn` to extract value based on the inflated validator reserve / deflated user reserve, or reenters `rebalanceSwap` again. 5) Attacker never actually pays `amountIn` (or pays less via reentrancy), draining userToken reserves.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of userToken reserves; pool insolvency; incorrect reserve accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move the `transferFrom` of `validatorToken` before reserve updates, and apply checks-effects-interactions (or a reentrancy guard) so reserves are only mutated after funds are received.

hypotheses.title: FeeSwap drains validator reserve at fixed rate ignoring pool ratio
hypotheses.description: executeFeeSwap() computes amountOut = amountIn * M / SCALE (a flat 99.7% rate) regardless of the pool's reserve ratio. Because the output is not derived from the constant-product invariant, an attacker can repeatedly swap userToken for validatorToken at a fixed favorable rate until reserveValidatorToken is exhausted, extracting value from LPs who deposited validatorToken.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker mints a minimal pool or targets an existing pool with validatorToken liquidity. 2) Calls executeFeeSwap with large amountIn of userToken. 3) Receives amountOut = 99.7% of amountIn in validatorToken. 4) Repeats until reserveValidatorToken is drained, leaving the pool with only userToken and LPs unable to withdraw their validatorToken.
hypotheses.impact: LPs lose their validatorToken deposits; pool becomes one-sided and insolvent for burn() withdrawals of validatorToken.
hypotheses.recommendation: Derive amountOut from the constant-product invariant using current reserves (x*y=k) rather than a fixed M/SCALE rate.

hypotheses.title: FeeAMM mint() ignores userToken deposit, mints liquidity for free
hypotheses.description: The mint() function only pulls `amountValidatorToken` from the caller but never transfers any `userToken` into the pool, yet it credits the pool with a reserve of userToken implicitly via the AMM invariant used in subsequent swaps. The pool's `reserveUserToken` is never increased during mint, so the pool is initialized with zero userToken reserve while liquidity shares are issued. This means the pool's accounting is inconsistent with actual token balances, and any userToken that later flows in via swaps is effectively free liquidity for the LP.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls mint() with a small amountValidatorToken, receiving liquidity shares. 2) Attacker then calls executeFeeSwap() with a large amountIn of userToken, which increases reserveUserToken and decreases reserveValidatorToken. 3) Attacker calls burn() to redeem liquidity shares, receiving a proportional share of the now-inflated reserveUserToken (which came from their own swap) plus reserveValidatorToken. 4) Because mint never required userToken deposit, the attacker can extract validatorToken from the pool without ever having provided userToken liquidity.
hypotheses.impact: Pool insolvency — LPs and the pool lose validatorToken reserves; attacker drains validatorToken for free.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require and transferFrom a proportional amount of userToken during mint, and update `pool.reserveUserToken` accordingly.

hypotheses.title: FeeAMM mint() does not update reserveUserToken, breaking AMM invariant
hypotheses.description: In mint(), only `pool.reserveValidatorToken` is incremented; `pool.reserveUserToken` is never touched. The liquidity calculation for subsequent mints uses `pool.reserveUserToken` in the denominator, so the pool's invariant is broken from the first mint. This means the pool's reserves do not reflect actual token holdings, and burn() will compute payouts against a reserve that was never funded.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker mints with a small validatorToken amount. 2) Attacker performs a fee swap to inject userToken into reserveUserToken. 3) Attacker burns liquidity shares to withdraw a proportional share of the injected userToken plus validatorToken, extracting value from the pool without having provided userToken at mint time.
hypotheses.impact: LP value extraction; pool insolvency; incorrect liquidity accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require and transfer userToken during mint, and increment `pool.reserveUserToken` by the deposited amount.

hypotheses.title: rebalanceSwap rate (N) is worse than feeSwap rate (M), enabling arbitrage
hypotheses.description: rebalanceSwap charges amountIn = amountOut * N / SCALE + 1 (99.85%+1) while executeFeeSwap pays out at M/SCALE (99.7%). The two rates are inconsistent with any invariant, so an attacker can chain swaps to extract value: obtain userToken cheaply via rebalanceSwap and sell it back via executeFeeSwap, or vice versa, at the protocol's expense.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls rebalanceSwap to receive amountOut userToken paying amountIn = amountOut*N/SCALE+1 validatorToken. 2) Calls executeFeeSwap with that userToken to receive amountOut2 = amountIn2*M/SCALE validatorToken. 3) If M/N spread and rounding allow profit, repeat; pool reserves are drained by the spread each cycle.
hypotheses.impact: Systematic value extraction from the pool reserves, depleting LP funds and breaking pool solvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a single consistent invariant-based pricing for both swap directions so no round-trip arbitrage exists.

hypotheses.title: FeeSwap drains validator reserve without updating user reserve correctly
hypotheses.description: executeFeeSwap credits `pool.reserveUserToken += amountIn` and debits `pool.reserveValidatorToken -= amountOut`, but the actual token transfer of `userToken` uses `transferFrom` which may not deliver exactly `amountIn` for fee-on-transfer tokens. The reserve accounting assumes the full amountIn arrives, so reserves drift from real holdings. Additionally, the swap rate M=9970 is applied to amountIn without any reserve-based pricing, meaning the pool can be drained of validatorToken at a fixed rate regardless of reserve ratio.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker uses a fee-on-transfer userToken (or a token that returns true but transfers less). 2) Calls executeFeeSwap with large amountIn. 3) Contract credits full amountIn to reserveUserToken but only receives amountIn - fee. 4) Attacker receives full amountOut of validatorToken. 5) Repeat until validatorToken reserve is drained; reserveUserToken overstates real balance.
hypotheses.impact: Validator token reserve drained; pool accounting inflated on user side; LPs and other swappers lose funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Measure actual received amount via balance delta before crediting reserves, and reject fee-on-transfer/rebasing tokens or account for them.

hypotheses.title: burn() pays out proportional reserves but mint() only took one side
hypotheses.description: burn() returns amountUserToken = liquidity * reserveUserToken / totalSupply and amountValidatorToken = liquidity * reserveValidatorToken / totalSupply. Since mint() only collected validatorToken but credited liquidity against a denominator that includes userToken reserves, the sum of all burn payouts can exceed what was actually deposited, making the pool insolvent for later burners.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker mints into a pool where reserveUserToken is large relative to reserveValidatorToken, receiving liquidity that entitles them to a share of the userToken reserve they never contributed to. 2) Attacker immediately burns, withdrawing userToken they did not deposit. 3) Remaining LPs find the pool under-collateralized and cannot withdraw their full share.
hypotheses.impact: Last withdrawers suffer loss; pool reserves are drained below totalSupply obligations.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure mint() deposits both tokens (or prices liquidity strictly on the deposited token) so that burn() payouts never exceed contributions.

hypotheses.title: mint() liquidity formula ignores userToken deposit, mispricing shares
hypotheses.description: mint() only pulls amountValidatorToken from the caller but computes liquidity using denom = reserveValidatorToken + (N * reserveUserToken)/SCALE, treating the userToken reserve as if it were validatorToken. A minter receives shares priced against a distorted denominator, so they can mint more liquidity than their deposit warrants, diluting existing LPs.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a pool with large reserveUserToken and small reserveValidatorToken. 2) Calls mint with a small amountValidatorToken. 3) Because denom is inflated by N*reserveUserToken/SCALE, liquidity = amountValidatorToken * totalSupply / denom is small — but the attacker can instead target pools where reserveUserToken is small to get disproportionately large liquidity per validatorToken deposited, then burn to withdraw a share of the large userToken reserve.
hypotheses.impact: Existing LPs' share of reserves is diluted; attacker extracts userToken value on burn.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute liquidity from the actual deposited amounts and current reserves using a consistent invariant (e.g., proportional to both reserves), not a formula that substitutes one reserve for the other.

hypotheses.title: mint liquidity calculation uses fixed N rate instead of reserve ratio
hypotheses.description: In the non-initial branch, liquidity = amountValidatorToken * _totalSupply / (reserveValidatorToken + N*reserveUserToken/SCALE). This uses the fixed N constant rather than the actual reserve ratio, so the LP share minted does not reflect the true value contributed relative to existing reserves. An attacker can mint at a favorable valuation when the pool ratio deviates from N/SCALE, then burn to extract more than deposited.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a pool where reserveUserToken/reserveValidatorToken deviates from SCALE/N. 2) Attacker mints a large amountValidatorToken, receiving liquidity computed with the fixed N rate. 3) Attacker immediately burns the liquidity, receiving a proportional share of both reserves. 4) Because the mint valuation was wrong, the attacker extracts more value than deposited.
hypotheses.impact: LP share mispricing leads to value extraction from existing LPs; pool accounting becomes inconsistent.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use the actual reserve ratio (reserveUserToken/reserveValidatorToken) when computing liquidity shares, or enforce that the pool ratio equals N/SCALE before minting.

hypotheses.title: burn returns proportional reserves but mint used fixed rate, enabling round-trip profit
hypotheses.description: burn pays out amountUserToken = liquidity*reserveUserToken/totalSupply and amountValidatorToken = liquidity*reserveValidatorToken/totalSupply, i.e., proportional to actual reserves. But mint priced new liquidity using the fixed N constant. This asymmetry means a mint-then-burn round trip is profitable whenever the pool ratio differs from N/SCALE, allowing an attacker to siphon reserves from existing LPs.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker identifies a pool whose reserve ratio deviates from N/SCALE. 2) Attacker mints liquidity (priced with fixed N). 3) Attacker burns the same liquidity (priced proportionally to actual reserves). 4) The difference is profit extracted from the pool.
hypotheses.impact: Existing LPs lose funds; pool reserves are drained via repeated round trips.
hypotheses.recommendation: Make mint and burn use consistent pricing (both based on actual reserves), or add a swap fee/slippage guard that prevents round-trip arbitrage.

hypotheses.title: executeFeeSwap() transfers output before/after state inconsistently and lacks reentrancy guard
hypotheses.description: `executeFeeSwap()` calls `IERC20(userToken).transferFrom(...)` (external call) before updating reserves, and then calls `IERC20(validatorToken).transfer(msg.sender, amountOut)` after updating reserves. A malicious `userToken` with a `transferFrom` hook can reenter while reserves are stale (pre-update), and a malicious `validatorToken` can reenter during the outbound transfer while reserves are already updated but the swap is not finalized. Combined with `checkSufficientLiquidity` being a view used by integrators, this enables read-only reentrancy and cross-function manipulation.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker uses a pool with a hookable `userToken`. 2) Calls `executeFeeSwap`; during `transferFrom`, the hook reenters `burn()` or `rebalanceSwap()` to exploit the not-yet-updated reserves (e.g., burn liquidity at favorable ratio). 3) Alternatively, during the outbound `validatorToken.transfer`, reenter `checkSufficientLiquidity`-dependent logic or another swap to observe/exploit the mid-state. 4) Profit from the reserve skew.
hypotheses.impact: Value extraction from LPs; incorrect swap pricing; potential insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard and follow checks-effects-interactions: update reserves before external transfers, and ensure `transferFrom` completes before any state mutation that other functions rely on.

hypotheses.title: First depositor can manipulate share price via direct token donation
hypotheses.description: On the first mint, liquidity = amountValidatorToken/2 - MIN_LIQUIDITY, and MIN_LIQUIDITY shares are minted to the pool (not to the depositor). However, reserves are only updated by the minted amount. An attacker can front-run the first legitimate minter by directly transferring userToken and/or validatorToken to the contract (donation), inflating reserves without minting shares. Then when the victim mints, the formula `liquidity = amountValidatorToken * totalSupply / denom` uses the inflated reserves, giving the victim far fewer shares than deserved. The attacker then burns their MIN_LIQUIDITY or later mints cheaply.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker sends tokens directly to FeeAMM contract for a fresh pool (reserves still 0 in storage, but token balance > 0). 2) Victim calls mint; formula uses storage reserves (still 0) so first-mint branch triggers — actually storage reserves are 0 so donation doesn't affect first mint. But after first mint, attacker donates to inflate reserves before victim's second mint. 3) Victim's liquidity = amountValidatorToken * totalSupply / (reserveValidatorToken + N*reserveUserToken/SCALE) with inflated reserves → tiny shares. 4) Attacker burns their shares for disproportionate assets.
hypotheses.impact: Victim receives near-zero shares for their deposit; attacker extracts victim's deposit.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track reserves via internal accounting only (already done) but also use balance-delta on mint to detect donations, or mint minimum liquidity to a burn address and use a virtual offset.

hypotheses.title: mint() credits liquidity before transferFrom completes; hookable token can reenter
hypotheses.description: `mint()` computes `liquidity`, then calls `IERC20(validatorToken).transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amountValidatorToken)` BEFORE updating `pool.reserveValidatorToken`, `totalSupply`, and `liquidityBalances`. A malicious `validatorToken` with a `transferFrom` hook can reenter `mint()`, `burn()`, or `rebalanceSwap()` while the pool reserves and totalSupply are stale, allowing manipulation of the liquidity calculation (which depends on `pool.reserveValidatorToken` and `_totalSupply`).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a pool with a hookable `validatorToken`. 2) Calls `mint()`; during `transferFrom`, the hook reenters `mint()` again. 3) Because `pool.reserveValidatorToken` and `totalSupply` have not been updated, the second `mint()` computes liquidity against stale values, over-crediting the attacker. 4) Attacker then burns the inflated liquidity to drain reserves.
hypotheses.impact: Over-minting of LP shares; dilution of existing LPs; reserve drainage.
hypotheses.recommendation: Update `pool.reserveValidatorToken`, `totalSupply`, and `liquidityBalances` before the `transferFrom`, or add a reentrancy guard.

hypotheses.title: executeFeeSwap has no liquidity-provider or pool-existence check
hypotheses.description: executeFeeSwap() is callable by anyone against any (userToken, validatorToken) pair, including pools that were never initialized. Because reserves default to zero, the require on reserveValidatorToken >= amountOut will revert for empty pools, but for any pool with reserves, any external actor can swap at the fixed M rate without any authorization or slippage protection. There is no check that the caller is a legitimate fee payer or that the pool is registered.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker monitors pools with validatorToken reserves. 2) Calls executeFeeSwap with amountIn sized so amountOut drains reserveValidatorToken. 3) Receives validatorToken at the fixed 99.7% rate, extracting value from LPs.
hypotheses.impact: LPs' validatorToken reserves can be systematically drained at a favorable fixed rate; pool economics broken.
hypotheses.recommendation: Gate executeFeeSwap to authorized fee-flow callers or add pool registration/whitelist checks.

hypotheses.title: burn() does not verify pool has enough tokens, can revert or underflow
hypotheses.description: `_calculateBurnAmounts` computes proportional amounts from storage reserves, but if actual token balances are lower than storage reserves (due to fee-on-transfer on prior deposits or direct transfers out), the `IERC20.transfer` calls will revert or transfer less. Also `pool.reserveUserToken -= uint128(amountUserToken)` can underflow if amountUserToken exceeds reserve due to rounding — though proportional math should prevent that. The real risk is storage reserves exceeding real balance, causing burn to fail (frozen funds) or transfer less than owed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker uses fee-on-transfer token to mint, so storage reserve > real balance. 2) Later, any LP tries to burn; transfer of amountUserToken fails or transfers less than computed. 3) LP cannot withdraw full value; funds effectively frozen or lost.
hypotheses.impact: LP funds frozen or under-redeemed; pool becomes insolvent relative to storage accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use actual balance deltas for all reserve updates and validate real balance >= storage reserve before burn.

hypotheses.title: checkSufficientLiquidity uses fixed M rate, misleading integrators
hypotheses.description: checkSufficientLiquidity computes amountOutNeeded = maxAmount * M / SCALE and checks reserveValidatorToken >= amountOutNeeded. This mirrors the fixed-rate logic in executeFeeSwap, so it does not reflect the true cost of a swap against the pool's actual reserves. Integrators relying on this view for slippage or liquidity checks will get incorrect results.
hypotheses.attackPath: An integrator calls checkSufficientLiquidity, sees it pass, then calls executeFeeSwap expecting the same amountOut. Because the pool ratio may differ from M/SCALE, the actual swap either reverts or pays a different amount than expected, causing integration failures or unexpected losses.
hypotheses.impact: Integrators may mis-size swaps, leading to reverts or unfavorable execution; no direct fund loss to the pool but can cause downstream losses.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the required output using the same invariant-based formula as the actual swap, so the view matches execution.

hypotheses.title: FeeAMM burn() reverts on zero transfer, trapping liquidity providers
hypotheses.description: `burn()` calls `IERC20(userToken).transfer(to, amountUserToken)` and `IERC20(validatorToken).transfer(to, amountValidatorToken)` unconditionally. When a pool's reserves become imbalanced (e.g., after many one-directional fee swaps or rebalance swaps), `_calculateBurnAmounts` can return 0 for one side. Many ERC20 implementations (and TIP-20 stablecoins) revert on zero-value transfers, causing `burn()` to revert and permanently blocking LP withdrawals.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker repeatedly calls `executeFeeSwap` in one direction to drain `reserveValidatorToken` toward zero while growing `reserveUserToken`. 2) When `reserveValidatorToken` is small relative to `totalSupply`, any LP's `burn()` computes `amountValidatorToken = liquidity * reserveValidatorToken / totalSupply == 0`. 3) The unconditional `transfer(to, 0)` reverts on tokens that disallow zero transfers, so LPs cannot withdraw their share of `reserveUserToken`.
hypotheses.impact: Liquidity providers are permanently unable to withdraw their funds from the pool; user-token reserves become stuck in the contract.
hypotheses.recommendation: Skip the transfer when the computed amount is zero (e.g., `if (amountUserToken != 0) IERC20(userToken).transfer(to, amountUserToken);` and same for validator token).

hypotheses.title: First-mint MIN_LIQUIDITY is added to totalSupply but not to any balance
hypotheses.description: On the first mint, totalSupply[poolId] += MIN_LIQUIDITY but liquidityBalances[poolId][to] is only credited with liquidity = amountValidatorToken/2 - MIN_LIQUIDITY. The MIN_LIQUIDITY shares are permanently unowned, so burn() payouts computed against totalSupply are systematically smaller than the reserves, and the unowned shares can never be burned — locking a proportional slice of reserves forever.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an attacker, but any LP burning shares receives less than their proportional reserve share because totalSupply includes the phantom MIN_LIQUIDITY. Over time the locked fraction grows relative to real shares as reserves accrue.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent lock of a fraction of pool reserves; LPs receive less than their fair share on burn.
hypotheses.recommendation: Either mint MIN_LIQUIDITY to a burn address (so it is accounted) or exclude it from totalSupply used in burn calculations.

hypotheses.title: FeeAMM checkSufficientLiquidity uses wrong formula vs executeFeeSwap
hypotheses.description: `checkSufficientLiquidity` computes `amountOutNeeded = (maxAmount * M) / SCALE`, but `executeFeeSwap` computes `amountOut = (amountIn * M) / SCALE`. The view function is meant to validate that a swap of `maxAmount` will succeed, but it uses the same formula as the swap — which is fine — except the naming and the fact that `maxAmount` is treated as `amountIn` while the check is against `reserveValidatorToken >= amountOutNeeded`. This is consistent, but the function is external and callers may assume `maxAmount` is the output amount. More importantly, the check does not account for the actual `amountIn` being transferred in, so a caller relying on this view can be misled if they pass the desired output as `maxAmount`.
hypotheses.attackPath: A caller (e.g., a router) uses checkSufficientLiquidity(userToken, validatorToken, desiredOut) to verify a swap will succeed, but the function interprets desiredOut as amountIn, so the check passes when the actual swap would revert or vice versa. This is a caller-side integration bug rather than a direct theft.
hypotheses.impact: Integration failure — swaps revert unexpectedly or pass checks that should fail, causing failed transactions or misrouted funds in dependent contracts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Rename parameter to `amountIn` and document clearly, or change the formula to match the intended semantics.

hypotheses.title: mint() allows arbitrary to address and uninitialized pool creation by anyone
hypotheses.description: mint() is fully public and lets any caller create a new pool for any token pair and mint liquidity to an arbitrary `to` address. There is no registry, whitelist, or owner check, so an attacker can seed pools with malicious or fake ERC20 tokens and later have other users interact with them. The first-minter also sets the initial price ratio implicitly.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a fake ERC20. 2) Calls mint(fakeToken, realToken, amount, attacker) to create a pool. 3) Subsequent users or integrations that trust pool existence may swap against the manipulated pool.
hypotheses.impact: Phishing/poisoned pools, manipulated initial pricing, potential loss for integrators that assume pools are legitimate.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict pool creation to a trusted registry or validate tokens against an allowlist.

hypotheses.title: rebalanceSwap amountIn rounding favors caller, drains pool over time
hypotheses.description: `amountIn = (amountOut * N) / SCALE + 1` rounds up, which is correct for the protocol, but the pool reserve update `pool.reserveValidatorToken += uint128(amountIn)` assumes the full amountIn is received. If validatorToken is fee-on-transfer, the pool credits more than received. Also, the `+1` is added unconditionally even when amountOut*N is exactly divisible, over-charging by 1 wei each call — minor but accumulates.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker repeatedly calls rebalanceSwap with tiny amountOut values; each call over-charges 1 wei of validatorToken relative to the exact rate, but more importantly if validatorToken has transfer fees, the pool credits amountIn while receiving less, letting attacker extract userToken at a discount.
hypotheses.impact: Slow reserve drift; with fee-on-transfer tokens, direct loss of userToken reserves.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use balance-delta accounting for received tokens; only add +1 when there is a remainder.

hypotheses.title: checkSufficientLiquidity uses M but executeFeeSwap can be front-run to drain
hypotheses.description: checkSufficientLiquidity() only verifies reserveValidatorToken >= maxAmount*M/SCALE at call time. Because executeFeeSwap has no per-caller limit and the rate is fixed, an attacker can front-run a legitimate swap by draining the validator reserve first, causing the victim's swap to revert (or execute at a worse effective rate if they retry), and the attacker captures the value.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim calls checkSufficientLiquidity and prepares a swap. 2) Attacker sees the pending tx, calls executeFeeSwap with a large amountIn to consume the validator reserve. 3) Victim's swap reverts with INSUFFICIENT_LIQUIDITY; attacker has extracted validatorToken at the fixed favorable rate.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing plus value extraction; victims' swaps fail and LPs' reserves are drained by the attacker.
hypotheses.recommendation: Price swaps via the invariant so large swaps move the price against the attacker, removing the incentive to front-run and drain.

hypotheses.title: checkSufficientLiquidity() is manipulable via same-block swap/rebalance ordering
hypotheses.description: `checkSufficientLiquidity()` is a view used by external integrators to verify that a pool can cover `maxAmount`. Because `executeFeeSwap()` and `rebalanceSwap()` mutate `reserveValidatorToken` within the same block, an attacker can front-run a victim's `checkSufficientLiquidity`-gated action by draining `reserveValidatorToken` via `executeFeeSwap` (or `rebalanceSwap`), causing the victim's check to fail or pass incorrectly, then back-run to restore the reserve and capture the victim's flow.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim intends to call an integrator that first calls `checkSufficientLiquidity(userToken, validatorToken, maxAmount)`. 2) Attacker observes the pending tx and front-runs with `executeFeeSwap` to reduce `reserveValidatorToken` below `amountOutNeeded`, making the victim's check revert (DoS) or, in the reverse direction, manipulates reserves so the victim's subsequent swap executes at a worse rate. 3) Attacker back-runs to restore reserves and profit from the sandwich.
hypotheses.impact: DoS of integrator flows; sandwich profit at victim's expense; stale/incorrect liquidity gating.
hypotheses.recommendation: Do not rely on a standalone view for liquidity gating; perform the check atomically inside the consuming function, and consider slippage/deadline parameters for swaps.

hypotheses.title: FeeAMM rebalanceSwap() can be griefed to drain user-token reserves
hypotheses.description: `rebalanceSwap` lets any caller exchange `validatorToken` for `userToken` at a fixed rate (`amountIn = amountOut * N / SCALE + 1`). There is no per-caller limit or cooldown, so an attacker can repeatedly drain `reserveUserToken` down to zero. Once `reserveUserToken == 0`, `executeFeeSwap` still works (it only checks validator reserve), but `burn()` for LPs returns zero user tokens and `rebalanceSwap` reverts with `INVALID_AMOUNT`, effectively freezing the pool's user-token side.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker acquires validatorToken. 2) Repeatedly calls `rebalanceSwap(userToken, validatorToken, amountOut, attacker)` to pull out all `reserveUserToken`. 3) Pool now has `reserveUserToken == 0`; LPs cannot burn meaningfully and the pool is one-sided.
hypotheses.impact: LP funds in the user-token side are drained at a favorable fixed rate; pool becomes unusable for the user-token side.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce a minimum reserve ratio or cap `amountOut` relative to `reserveUserToken` (e.g., require `pool.reserveUserToken - amountOut >= MIN_LIQUIDITY`).

hypotheses.title: burn() sends both tokens to caller-chosen `to` without ownership check
hypotheses.description: burn() correctly debits liquidityBalances[poolId][msg.sender], but the output tokens are sent to an arbitrary `to` address supplied by the caller. While the caller must own the liquidity, the lack of any restriction on `to` combined with no reentrancy guard on the ERC20 transfers allows a malicious token to reenter burn/mint/swap during the transfer and manipulate pool state.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a malicious userToken or validatorToken with a reentrant transfer hook. 2) Calls burn() with that token in the pool. 3) During IERC20.transfer, the hook reenters executeFeeSwap or rebalanceSwap to extract value before reserves are decremented.
hypotheses.impact: State inconsistency and potential reserve drainage via reentrancy; wrong accounting of reserves vs. balances.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a nonReentrant guard and/or use a pull-pattern for withdrawals; validate `to` if intended to be restricted.

hypotheses.title: FeeAMM executeFeeSwap() can drain validator reserve to zero, blocking rebalance
hypotheses.description: `executeFeeSwap` only requires `pool.reserveValidatorToken >= amountOut`. An attacker can repeatedly swap in userToken to drain `reserveValidatorToken` to exactly zero. Once zero, `rebalanceSwap` (which requires `pool.reserveUserToken >= amountOut` and adds to validator reserve) still works, but `checkSufficientLiquidity` and any downstream fee-swap flow revert. More importantly, LPs calling `burn()` will get `amountValidatorToken == 0`, and if the validator token reverts on zero transfers, burn is blocked.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains userToken. 2) Repeatedly calls `executeFeeSwap` until `reserveValidatorToken == 0`. 3) LP `burn()` now computes zero validator payout; on tokens that revert on zero transfer, burn reverts, trapping LP user-token share.
hypotheses.impact: LP withdrawals blocked; pool's validator side drained; protocol fee-swap functionality halted.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require a minimum remaining validator reserve after swaps, or handle zero-amount transfers in `burn()`.

hypotheses.title: FeeAMM burn() uses stale totalSupply causing rounding to zero
hypotheses.description: `_calculateBurnAmounts` divides by `totalSupply[poolId]`. If a pool has very small reserves relative to totalSupply (e.g., after a large rebalanceSwap drains user reserve), a small LP's `liquidity * reserve / totalSupply` rounds to zero for one or both tokens, and the unconditional transfers revert on zero-transfer tokens, blocking the burn.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker drains one reserve via rebalanceSwap/executeFeeSwap. 2) Small LP calls burn; computed amount is 0; transfer reverts.
hypotheses.impact: Small LPs cannot withdraw; funds stuck.
hypotheses.recommendation: Guard zero-amount transfers in `burn()`.
